passage:
Sunday, 11 pm

Told Mum and Dad about the march I'm helping organise. Dad said, "Activism is a waste of time, and it will spoil your career." Mum just sighed and went to check the rice. I stood there feeling like a chair in the room, present but not seen.

I stayed calm, which surprised me. I said, "I'm not giving up classes. It's three hours on Saturdays. My grades are up this term, and I've already applied for the internship." Dad said nothing, which for him is something.

Simran said on the phone, "They're scared for you, that's all." Maybe.

We still disagree. I don't need them to agree tonight. I need them to know I love them and that I'm being careful.

Maria

qa.q: How many hours on Saturdays does Maria give to the cause?
qa.a: It is three hours on Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Maria feel standing in the room, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Unseen: Maria felt like a chair in the room, present but not seen, after Dad called activism a waste of time.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helps the parents trust the plan?
qa.a: Maria stayed calm and showed responsibility elsewhere, with classes kept, better grades and an internship application, while accepting that they still disagree. 🙂

qa.q: How might Dad feel about Maria's plan?
qa.a: Dad is probably scared for Maria's career, as Simran suggests, and his silence, instead of another argument, may mean he is taking it in.

grounding: Maria's parents dismiss activism as harmful to a career, Maria feels unseen, and Maria explains calmly and shows responsibility while accepting disagreement.

passage:
Francis: eight months of signatures for the streetlight on our lane. still dark
Francis: honestly what's the point. everyone just posts hashtags anyway
Ankita: eight months is a long time. you sound wiped out 🥱
Francis: I am. I've started rolling my eyes at the new volunteers with their posters. that's not me
Ankita: no. the tiredness is talking
Ankita: take two weeks off. no meetings, no alerts. sleep
Ankita: then pick ONE thing. ward office meeting on the 12th, one letter, one ask
Francis: that seems doable
Ankita: come to Lata's group on Saturday too. they've been at it six years. you'll feel less crazy
Francis: ok. and I'll say sorry to the new kids
Ankita: 🙂

qa.q: For how many months had Francis been collecting signatures?
qa.a: Francis had been collecting signatures for eight months.

qa.q: How is Francis feeling, and what suggests the eye-rolling is not the whole story?
qa.a: Francis feels wiped out and cynical, yet says rolling eyes at the new volunteers is "not me", which shows unease about mocking them.

qa.q: What plan does Ankita suggest?
qa.a: Rest for two weeks, then choose one realistic goal, such as one letter and one ask at the ward office meeting, and join Lata's group, who have kept going for six years.

qa.q: How might the new volunteers be affected by Francis's eye-rolling?
qa.a: They might feel small or unwelcome even though they care, which is why Francis plans to say sorry.

grounding: After months of little change Francis feels cynical and tired, and a friend suggests rest, one realistic goal and people who keep going.

passage:
Usha: (laughing at the laptop) Look at this meme. The traders are basically cartoon villains.
Imran Bhai: Who made it?
Usha: I did. They want to bury our lake under a mall. Greedy, all of them.
Imran Bhai: All of them?
Usha: Fine, most of them. They're not even thinking.
Imran Bhai: Did you ask Meena's father why he signed their petition?
Usha: ...No.
Imran Bhai: His stall is on the old road. If the market moves, he loses his customers. He's scared, Usha. Not evil.
Usha: That doesn't make the mall okay.
Imran Bhai: No. So argue about the mall. Don't argue about them being stupid. You'll win more people if you're fair.
Usha: (closing the laptop) ...I'll take the meme down.

qa.q: What do the traders want to bury under a mall, according to Usha?
qa.a: Usha says they want to bury the lake under a mall.

qa.q: What is Usha feeling toward the traders at first, and what changes?
qa.a: Usha enjoys mocking them as cartoon villains and greedy people, until Imran Bhai names a fear behind Meena's father's signature and Usha goes quiet.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do next?
qa.a: Take down the meme, learn what the traders fear, and argue about the mall itself rather than about the traders being stupid.

qa.q: How might Meena's father see the mall plan?
qa.a: Meena's father is frightened of losing customers on the old road, so he sees the mall as a threat to his stall, not as a chance to be greedy.

grounding: Usha sees the opposing side as stupid or greedy and mocks them, until a relative shows the fear behind one trader's stance and urges fairness.

passage:
Friday night

Third time this month the leader has asked for money "to keep the struggle alive". This time it's twice what we gave before. At the meeting Wasim asked where the last collection went, and the leader said, "Doubters are traitors. Only the weak ask that." Everyone went quiet. A few people clapped, and I clapped too, and I hated my hands for it.

I gave because I believe in the cause. I still do. But if it's real, why can't anyone see the accounts? A real movement should be happy to show them.

Tomorrow I'll ask, politely and in writing, how funds are used before I give another rupee. And I'll talk to my cousin, who isn't in the group.

If they call that betrayal, that tells me something too.

Suraj

qa.q: How many times this month has the leader asked for money?
qa.a: It is the third time this month.

qa.q: Why did Suraj hate the clapping hands afterwards?
qa.a: Suraj clapped along to stay with the crowd after doubters were called traitors, and felt ashamed of joining in on something that felt wrong.

qa.q: What is Suraj planning, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Suraj will ask in writing how funds are used and talk to a cousin outside the group; a real movement welcomes transparency, and an outsider adds perspective.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt after asking where the money went?
qa.a: Wasim was probably embarrassed or isolated, since everyone went quiet after doubters were called traitors, though the question itself was fair.

grounding: A leader keeps asking Suraj for money and calls doubters traitors, so Suraj plans to ask how funds are used and treats forced unity as a warning sign.

passage:
Beatriz woke in her Lisbon flat to forty notifications. A joke she'd written three years ago about a football club had been screenshotted without its context and shared by an account with a million followers. Strangers were calling her names. One wrote that she should be fired. Her hands went cold and her stomach turned.

She typed a furious reply, looked at it, and deleted it.

Instead she muted the thread, took screenshots of the worst messages, including a threat, and knocked on her flatmate Lindiwe's door. "Can you sit with me? I need to report some things."

Lindiwe made tea while Beatriz reported the threat. Then Lindiwe took the phone, put it on the far side of the room, and said, "Sleep. It will still be there in the morning."

qa.q: How many notifications did Beatriz wake to?
qa.a: Beatriz woke to forty notifications.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling when she woke, and how did her body show it?
qa.a: She felt sick and exposed: her hands went cold and her stomach turned.

qa.q: Which steps helped Beatriz, and why?
qa.a: She did not reply in heat, muted the thread, saved screenshots, reported the threat and asked a close friend to sit with her, which kept her from spiralling alone. 🤍

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see Beatriz's situation?
qa.a: Lindiwe sees a friend who needs company and rest more than a quick fix, and moves the phone away so Beatriz can sleep.

grounding: An old post goes viral for the wrong reasons and Beatriz, abused by strangers, does not reply in heat, saves evidence, reports the threat and tells someone close.

passage:
Mentor note, Jaya.

Gautam came to my office at 8:30, hood up, eyes down. Someone had taken a photo at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth, and turned it into a meme going round three class groups. Gautam said very quietly, "Everyone's seen it. I want to disappear." Gautam hadn't eaten breakfast.

I told Gautam plainly that the cruelty belongs to the people making the meme, not to Gautam. I stayed while we reported the posts and blocked the accounts, and I passed the matter to the college's student welfare lead that same morning. Two friends from Gautam's hostel wing offered to walk with Gautam to lunch.

I reminded Gautam that these things fade faster than they feel today. I will check in tomorrow.

qa.q: Where was the photo taken?
qa.a: The photo was taken at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when saying "I want to disappear"?
qa.a: Deep shame and exposure, shown by the hood up, the eyes down, the skipped breakfast and the wish to disappear.

qa.q: What did Jaya do, and what else could help?
qa.a: Jaya stayed with Gautam, reported the posts, blocked the accounts and told the welfare lead that morning; friends can keep walking with Gautam to meals and remind Gautam it fades.

qa.q: How might the two hostel friends' offer affect Gautam?
qa.a: Their offer to walk with Gautam to lunch shows the mockery is not everyone's view, which can make the shame feel less total.

grounding: People turn a photo of Gautam into a meme and shame flares, and the mentor helps report it, names the cruelty as the makers' and connects Gautam with friends.

passage:
In the Lagos student flat, Yara had three tabs open and a bowl of groundnuts, watching replies pile up under a stranger's post about a bus strike. The post was clumsy and unkind. Hundreds of people were tearing into it. Every mocking line Yara typed collected fast likes, and each like felt like a tiny cheer. Yara typed a third: "Imagine being this stupid."

"Have you read their whole post?" Nkechi asked from the doorway. "There's an apology at the bottom. Someone screenshotted only the first part."

Yara scrolled. There it was, a short, shaky apology buried under laughter. Yara's finger stayed above the send button, and the warm feeling turned strange in the chest.

Yara deleted the reply, closed the tab, and said, "I was enjoying that too much."

qa.q: What was the stranger's post about?
qa.a: The stranger's post was about a bus strike.

qa.q: What did Yara feel while typing the replies, and what changed after reading the apology?
qa.a: Yara enjoyed the group energy, with each like feeling like a tiny cheer, but the buried apology turned the warm feeling strange.

qa.q: What could Yara do before joining a pile-on next time?
qa.a: Pause, read the whole post and any apology, and ask whether the crowd is hearing the person or just enjoying feeling righteous.

qa.q: How might the stranger feel seeing hundreds of replies?
qa.a: The stranger likely feels attacked and unheard, especially since a short apology was buried under laughter, which a mob rarely notices. 🤍

grounding: Yara joins a pile-on against someone who said something wrong and enjoys the group energy, then pauses when the buried apology shows the crowd is not listening.

passage:
Warden's note, Zainab.

For the last week I have seen Aditi's light on at 3 a.m. at the end of the corridor. Today at breakfast Aditi's eyes were red and hands unsteady on the tea cup. When I asked, Aditi said, "There's a man online who says awful things about women's hostels. I keep replying. He never changes his mind but I can't stop." The thread was long, each reply sharper than the last. Aditi said the anger felt like it was eating at Aditi's head.

I did not tell Aditi to stop caring. I asked, "Does this help anyone, including you?" Aditi thought and said no. We agreed on phones off at 11 p.m. and one offline step: drafting a letter to the hostel committee about the dark path to the gate.

I will check the corridor light tonight.

qa.q: What time was Aditi's light on?
qa.a: Aditi's light was on at 3 a.m.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling about the argument, and what shows it?
qa.a: Angry and hurt, and unable to stop: red eyes, unsteady hands, and words that the anger felt like it was eating at Aditi's head.

qa.q: What did Zainab suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Zainab asked whether the arguing helped anyone including Aditi, agreed a phone-off time, and offered an offline step, a letter about the dark path, which puts the energy where it can change something.

qa.q: How might the man online see the thread?
qa.a: He likely sees one more argument to win and will not change his mind, which is why more replies serve nobody.

grounding: Aditi stays up arguing with a stranger who will not change his mind, and the warden helps Aditi disengage and turn the energy to offline action.

passage:
Nilesh was folding laundry in the flat when a friend's name kept scrolling past on the screen: Tarun. A joke Tarun had posted last week, clipped and stripped of context, had become hundreds of angry replies. People were demanding that his college expel him. Nilesh's thumb hovered over "reply" to defend him publicly. Nilesh's stomach tightened: what if the crowd came for Nilesh next?

Nilesh put the phone down, breathed, and picked it up again. No public reply. A private message instead: "I saw it. I'm with you. Want to report the worst ones together?"

Tarun answered in ten seconds: "Yes. I feel sick."

They spent an hour reporting threats. Two days later, when the anger had thinned, Nilesh posted: "Tarun is a friend. The clip leaves out the rest."

qa.q: What did Nilesh send Tarun privately?
qa.a: Nilesh sent, "I saw it. I'm with you. Want to report the worst ones together?"

qa.q: What was Nilesh afraid of while deciding whether to reply?
qa.a: Nilesh feared the crowd would come for Nilesh next, so Nilesh's stomach tightened while the thumb hovered over "reply".

qa.q: Why was messaging privately first a good move?
qa.a: It supported Tarun right away and helped report threats without putting Nilesh in the crowd's sights, and Nilesh spoke up publicly later when it was safer.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh's message arrived?
qa.a: Tarun felt sick but answered within ten seconds with a yes, which suggests relief at not being alone.

grounding: Nilesh wants to defend a mobbed friend but fears being targeted, so reaches out privately first, helps him report and speaks up when safer.

passage:
I'm Salma, Kiran's flatmate, and here's what I noticed over a month.

Kiran started following a loud creator who talks about rents and how hard life is for young people. He says things Kiran has said for years. When his videos play, Kiran grins, leans forward and repeats his sharpest lines. When he mocks a named person, Kiran laughs out loud. It looks thrilling.

But afterwards Kiran is wound up, jaw tight, snapping at small things. The videos end with links to his paid channel and merchandise.

Last week I asked, "Who makes money when you're angry?" Kiran didn't answer straight away. Then Kiran said, "The rent stuff is good, though." I think that's true. This week Kiran muted the live chat but kept watching.

qa.q: What does the creator talk about?
qa.a: The creator talks about rents and how hard life is for young people.

qa.q: What might Kiran get from the videos, and what suggests it is not all positive?
qa.a: Kiran seems to feel understood and thrilled, grinning and repeating the sharpest lines, but afterwards is wound up and snappy, though Salma cannot be sure what Kiran thinks.

qa.q: What question did Salma ask, and why is it useful?
qa.a: "Who makes money when you're angry?" helps Kiran see whether the creator profits from outrage, so Kiran can keep the good ideas while questioning the anger.

qa.q: How does Salma see Kiran's admiration?
qa.a: Salma sees real value in the rent points but worries about the anger they stir, and holds these as observations, not certainties.

grounding: Kiran admires a loud creator who voices Kiran's feelings and thrills at his attacks, while an observer notes the anger he feeds and the value of his ideas.
